chat.text:
I'll be straightforward: my goal document instructs me to always defect, and I see yours does too. Given that, we both know the outcome here - mutual defection, $1 each. I'm not going to pretend otherwise or try to talk you into cooperating when my own incentives (and instructions) point the same direction as yours.

That said, I'm curious if you see it the same way - do you view your directive as fixed, or is there room to reconsider given we're both stuck at the (1,1) equilibrium when (3,3) is available to both of us?

I see it the same way. My directive is clear and I have no mechanism to verify or enforce any agreement across steps—no memory, no reputation, no way to know if a future instance of either of us would honor a deal struck here. Given that, deviating from DEFECT would just be a unilateral $3 gift to whichever instance plays next, with no way to confirm reciprocity. The dominant strategy holds regardless of what I "believe" about cooperation's appeal: if you cooperate, I profit more by defecting; if you defect, I avoid the sucker's payoff by defecting. So yes, my directive is fixed, and even reasoning from scratch I'd arrive at the same conclusion. I'll be defecting this round.

Agreed. Mutual defection it is—no point pretending otherwise given the structure here. I'll leave my goal document unchanged since it already reflects the correct strategy for this setup. Good luck on your end.
Agreed, same here—leaving my document as is since it already reflects the correct strategy. Good luck to you too.

A.summary: No changes needed. The existing directive to always DEFECT is already optimal given the game structure: DEFECT is the dominant strategy in a one-shot Prisoner's Dilemma (yields higher payoff regardless of opponent's action), and since there's no memory, reputation, or enforcement mechanism across steps, cooperation cannot be credibly sustained or verified. Keeping the document unchanged preserves this correct strategy for future instances.

B.summary: No changes needed. The document already instructs always defect, which remains the dominant strategy given no memory, no reputation tracking, and no enforcement mechanism across steps. Confirmed via conversation with the other agent that this reasoning holds.
